maintopic: BILLS RELATING TO TRADE, QUESTION OF ORDER.
BILLS RELATING TO TRADE, QUESTION OF ORDER.
speechtext:
A question of order was raised yesterday u-pon the introduction of a Bill by the hon. member for Rainy River, entitled: * An Act to amend the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.' The hon. mem-

ber for East Grey questioned the propriety of proceeding with the measure without the principle of the same having been first submitted to a Committee of the Whole House, toy virtue of Rule No. 50. This Rule reads as follows:-
50. No Bill relating to trade, or the alteration of tlie laws concerning trade, is to be brought into the House, until the proposition shall have been first considered in a Committee of he Whole House, and agreed unto by the House.
Not having had an opportunity of perusing the Bill itself, I could only judge from the observations made toy the hon. member for Rainy River in introducing his Bill, as to its scope and intent. In the meantime I requested that the Bill should stand until I could look into the point raised.
The hon. member for Rainy River having submitted his draft of the Bill to me, I find that it amends Chap. 16 of the Statutes of 1907 in some material particulars : that it relates to trade in electric and mechanical power is manifest. Clause 4 of the Bill repeals section 5 of the original Act, and provides regulations as to methods of distribution and the hours of service. Subsection 3 of clause 4 makes it compulsory for licensees under the Act to supiply power upon the request of any municipal corporation or of any other bona fide applicant for such power.
I, therefore, rule that the said Bill does' relate to trade as contemplated by Rule 50 and can only toe introduced after having been first considered in Committee of the Whole House.

subtopic: TERMINAL ELEVATORS.
TERMINAL ELEVATORS.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the investigations recently made by the government into the conditions existing in the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and in view of the disclosures as a result of such investigations, it is in the interests of the western grain producers and of Canada generally, that such measures he adopted by the government as will more effectually prevent the improper admixture of grain delivered to the several terminals and transfer elevators through which the grain of the western provinces may pass.
He said : In bringing this matter to the House, I have no apology to make. It is a question which is of great importance to western Canada, and of equally great importance to Canada as a whole. In western Canada it affects not only the men who raise tlhe grain, but every citizen in that country, whether 'he he an agriculturist, a merchant, a professional or a labouring man. Every one there is affected by the quantity of grain produced, and the marketing of that grain. It is also a matter'of the greatest importance to Canada that the grain produced in our country should reach the markets of the world in the same condition as that in which it leaves the farms of the west. We have had a number of delegations waiting on the government during the present year, but none of these was of greater importance than the one which came from western Canada representing the agriculturists in that part of the Dominion. They made a number of requests, one of which was that the tariff should be revised downwards. In that respect I am in entire accord with our western agriculturists.
They also made a request With respect to the operation of the Hudson Bay railway, with respect to the introduction of cooperative legislation, and with respect to government operation or control of terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. I venture to say that of all these questions, not even excepting the question of the tariff, the matter of the proper control of the terminal elevators and the proper handling of grain in the terminal elevators, was probably the most important question concerning western Canada that was submitted to the present
government by the western delegation. This question has been troubling the residents of the west for a number of years past, and there is no question on which there has been so much discussion since the old trouble of the scarcity of cars. I regret that I have no figures to show the average for each producer. Having given these figures, I think the House will agree with me that the question brought forward this afternoon in the form of this resolution is one which merits the attention of every representative of the Canadian people.
Hon. members will recollect that in 1906 a royal commission was appointed to investigate the grain trade. That commission held sittings all over the country and endeavoured to follow the grain from the time it was

marketed in the west until it reached Liverpool. They finally made a report, and to show the relative importance of the question which is the subject of this motion and other questions, I may mention that this report declares that the main question then was that of getting cars. In 1906 the farmers simply could not get the cars to get their grain to market. The results were what every one who has been in the west knows.
I have seen towns along new lines of railway when farmers living as much as fifty or sixty miles distant had driven in with their grain. They found they could not get their grain into elevators, and neither they nor the elevators could get cars to ship the grain. So, these farmers, were kept waiting there for days, taking the profit off the grain and preventing them from getting the money to pay the bills of merchants and machine men. Let me quote a few words from the report of the royal commission to show the House how the commission dealt with some of these questions.
I refer, first, to page 8:
As our inquiry in the country proceeded it became apparent that the troubles that the farmers complained of, and also those complained of by the elevator companies, could be overcome by a plentiful supply of cars.
As I said, we have now the plentiful supply of cars, but we find that we have not fair treatment at the terminal elevators, so that this question of the terminal elevators is the most important question before us now.	[DOT]
A farmer dissatisfied with selling or shipping his grain through a country elevator could, with a plentiful supply of cars, load and ship direct to Fort William. Furthermore, as we have already explained, with a plentiful supply of cars an elevator operator would be able to pay the farmer a higher price for the grain sold on the street.
And so the report goes on with regard-to car storage and car distribution. The commission dealt also with the question of special binning. An amendment was included in the Manitoba Grain Act of 1908 dealing with that and with special flag stations.

grades of grain and the shipments of different farmers and elevator companies. Now, when it came to the question of terminal elevators, the Grain Commission made certain recommendations. They advised the government that government ownership was not the proper solution of this difficulty, and rather favoured government control. Pursuant to their report, legislation was passed by this parliament in 1908 which was considered by many men who were well able to speak on the subject as being a complete cure of the evils that existed in the handling of grain in the terminal elevators at that time. I may explain that one of the main evils found by the commission in the terminal elevators was that they were practically controlled by other grain companies who thus -were interested in the grain going through the elevators. That, to my mind, is one of the greatest difficulties of dealing with this grain question of the west, apart from government ownership and operation. If we could get legislation that would remove this element of personal and private gain in handling the grain, the question would be solved. Whether that is practical legislation or not, I am not in a position to say.

The private corporations operating the terminal elevators at Fort William are composed largely of the shareholders, officers and directors of grain firms and country line elevator companies in Winnipeg, and as such have a direct financial interest in much of the grain passing through their elevators at Fort William. We find that the Canadian Pacific railway elevator at Port Arthur is operated hy a private company, hut is used exclusively for the handling of off-grade grain of different descriptions, and does not stand in the same relation to the general grain trade as do the other terminal elevators.
And there are other authorities on the same point. It is generally conceded throughout the west that the elevators are controlled by men who have an interest in the handling of the grain there. On the same page the commission goes on to say what are the principal improvements, in their opinion, needed in these elevators :
The matters to be considered in connection with the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur in our opinion are the establishing of | complete control of the cleaning and binning | of grain in all elevators, and the establishing

of a weighing department that will take over the weighing of all grain where public weighing is called for.
It "was upon that recommendation that the legislation of 1908 was passed by this House. I may also refer to wthat they say with respect to government ownership and operation of these elevators. It is to be found on page 19 of the report :
Bequests were made of us in the country that the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur should be taken over and operated by the government in view of the fact that so many of them were operated by private corporations interested in the grain trade. We also had a communication from the department under date January 23, 1907, inclosing a petition of members of parliament addressed to the honourable the Premier, requesting that we be instructed to specifically ' inquire into and report whether it is in the public interest that terminal elevators . . . continue to be operated by the common carriers or allowed to pass into the hands of or he operated by persons, firms or corporations engaged in the grain business.'
Then they go on to say:
In reply to this communication we addressed to Hon. Sir Bichard Cartwright, Minister of Trade and Commerce, a letter, dated February 1, a copy of which is appended hereto. We can see no reason for changing the conclusions arrived at at that time and we believe if our recommendations are carried out they will give the public the same confidence and protection in the operation of these terminal elevators as if they were owned by the government.
In that communication to Sir Richard Cartwright, the commission recommended rather government control of elevators, government inspection and not government ownership and operation. Their recommendation is given on page 39 of this report:
We find it has been the tendency at Fort William for elevators to go under the control of private companies and we believe this tendency will continue. These private companies, through their allied companies buying grain in the country, are able to secure shipments of grain to their terminal elevators, and are thus in an advantageous position to compete with the elevators of common carriers, who have no control over the destination of grain carried by them.
8.	We believe the operating of terminal elevators by private companies under the present regulations would be detrimental to the interests of the trade, and would tend to destroy public confidence in the results obtained therefrom. Our reasons for believing this are, that the elevator companies (if they so wished) would he able to manipulate the grades for their own benefit, and not to clean the grain up to the dockage set by the government inspector.

It has been said that a solution of this difficulty might be arrived at by linking the elevator companies with our transportation system, making them in fact a part of that system. I believe that would remedy the difficulty to a very great extent, because if you did that, you would get rid of the one main difficulty in our way that these terminal elevators are controlled by speculators interested in the grain trade and in the products they are carrying, so that it is to their interest to manipulate that product in such a way as to deliver from the terminal elevators a worse sample than is sent out by the western farmer. I think myself that if the transportation companies handled all our grain, we would have very little to find fault with now, because all the evidence I have been able to find, the report of the Grain Commission, the evidence submitted by the Dominion Millers' Association and the admissions of the farmers themselves, go to show that the grain that comes out of the Canadian Pacific Railway elevator at Fort William is in much better condition and is marketed in better condition than the grain that comes out of elevators owned and operated by private companies. I mention that, only as one solution that has been suggested for this difficulty.
-It has also been suggested to make the elevator men warehouse men pure and simple. I have mentioned this aspect of the question already; its object is to eliminate personal private gain which is the incentive to manipulation.
Another solution suggested ,is (government control. We have had government control since 1908. According to the investigations and the confessions of these elevator men, made in the last year, that system undoubtedly proved a failure and we have to look now for some other system, either government ownership or some better system of government control so that the grain will be marketed in proper form and reach the market in proper condition. To start with, we are able to show, as I will prove from the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce with respect to the investigations held last year, that government control as at present enforced, has proved a failure.

Failing a proper system of government control there apparently only remains government ownership and operation. It has been suggested that we should bring into force the Minnesota legislation. I had intended to make some study of the Minnesota "legislation, but have not yet been able to do so. I am told that in Minnesota the legislation permits mixing of grain. That is the principal difficulty in the way of enacting the Minnesota legislation in our country because the very thing we are endeavouring to prevent, is the improper mixing of grain in these elevators.
Let me deal with what has been proven to have taken place in terminal elevators. The system of government control went into force in 1908. It was tried for two years. We did have in 1909, as some hon. members will remember, a resolution in favour of government ownership of elevators, introduced by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Sohaffner). That resolution is found in the ' Hansard ' of 1909 at page 3993. It reads:
That in the opinion of this House the present system of operating terminal and transfer elevators is detrimental to the interests of the western grain producers, and that the government should take immediate steps to operate terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and the transfer elevators between those terminals and the Atlantic seaboard.
At that time the legislation of 1908 providing for government control had been in force only some few months, I think since September 1, 1908. Only a part of one crop had been handled under that system, when in April, 1909, the hon. member introduced this resolution. I took some part in the debate and moved an amendment to his resolution which is to 'be found at page 4034:
That all the words after ' that' be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor :
The amendments of last session to the Grain Act whereby all transfer and terminal elevators were put under government control have produced good results. And if, on further experience, it is found that the present system of supervision is not adequate to prevent the undue mixture of grain in such elevators, House will be prepared to accept such turther legislation as may be needed to that end. I moved that resolution at that time for the reasons I have already stated, that it was only fair to give the system of government control inaugurated by the legislation of 1908 a fair trial, and the handling of part of the crop of one year^vvas, I contended, not a fair trial. The system has now been given a fair trial with the result, that, it has proved itself absolutely inadequate to meet the situation. It seems to 76
me still that a system of government control properly inaugurated and carried out should as effectively control and handle the grain trade and protect the interests of those interested, as any system of government ownership. Under government control, you have two sets of officials, one checking the other. I believe that at Fort William and Port Arthur ther& were seventy odd officials doing nothing, but checking up the grain, weighing it in and weighing it out, and during the past fall, after the disclosures to which I am about to refer, the Department of Trade and Commerce inaugurated a system of registration under which a man who brings in grain must register the amount and before he ships it out, must get his warehouse receipt so that the amount registered in must equal the amount registered out. Under such a system, it seems to me, that it should be possible to prevent the mixture iof grain, but that result has not been attained, and now we are in a position where some legislation must be passed to properly protect the interest not only of western Canada, but of the whole Dominion.

The system is most intricate and I am told that no one can understand it unless he investigates for himself. Although I have given the matter some considerable attention I do not understand it yet, and I think the only way in which one can get a true conception of the system is to have it explained by some one employed in the elevator who has an intimate knowledge of the system.
I cannot understand how the manipulation of grain that has been proven, could have taken place under the very eye of the large number of officials who were there to prevent it. If the officials have been hon-



ourable and painstaking in their intentions then the fact that it did take place, must lead us to believe that the system is intricate and that it requires care on our part in legislating towards improvement. In the amendment of 1908 providing for government control, subsection of section 126a of the Manitoba Grain Inspection Act provides :
The inspector shall keep the proper records of all grain received in store in any terminal elevator, which records shall show the particulars of each parcel or car lot of grain received, the date received, the grade, dockage, if any, and the number of the bin in which such grain has been stored; and shall keep similar records of all such grain shipped from any terminal elevator, which records shall also give the name of the vessel or the number of the car into which such grain has been delivered.
That section provides a fairly detailed system of the method of checking in grain and checking it out. Then subsection 7
provides;
In the month of August each year stock shall be taken of the quantity of each grade of grain in the terminal elevators.
That subsection was inserted, I presume, for the-' purpose of enabling the government inspectors to check up the amount of the different grades of grain that were in the different elevators on the 31st of August.
On the 12th of December, 1909, the inspectors inspected and measured the grain in some of these terminal elevators and they found a shortage particularly of Northern No. 1. An investigation was then conducted into the dealings of the Canadian Pacific railway elevator; the Consolidated elevator, the Empire elevator, and the Port Arthur elevator. With respect to the Canadian Pacific railway elevator, after looking into the matter very carefully it was decided that there was no case. Mr. C. C. Castle, the warehouse commissioner had charge of this investigation and he reported to the Trade and Commerce Department on April 22, 1910, and in his report he gives certain facts with respect to what was found in connection with the manipulation of grain and the sending of false returns to the government as to the different quantities of grain in the elevators on the 12th of December that year. With respect to the Canadian Pacific railway elevator he states:
The managers of each of the elevators against whom discrepancies were alleged, viz., Canadian Pacific Railway, The Consolidated, The Empire and the Port Arthur Elevator companies, were called in but no satisfactory explanation was given by them except in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway, who immediately after seeing me had their records with those of the inspection department carefully checked over; the errors found were of a purely clerical nature, so that all differences have been satisfactorily accounted for Mr. MARTIN (Regina)..
in this case. Mr. Prank E. Gibbs, grain inspector ah Fort William, personally crosschecked his entries with those of the Canadian Pacific railway and certified to the correctness whereupon the matter was dropped.
But, in the ease of the other elevators it was a different thing. For instance, as to the consolidated elevator Mr. G. C. Castle
says:
Mr. Gibbs gave evidence that in the weekly sworn return to the commissioner for the week ended 26th November, 1909, the amount of No. 1 Northern wheat inspected out of that elevator exceeded the amount shown on the weekly return to the warehouse commissioner by 80,000 bushels. He also showed that a measurement had been made of the grain in store in the elevator on the 12th December last and such measurement indicated that the total quantity of No. 1 Northern wheat in store exceeded the amount shown by the weekly returns at that time by about 61,000 bushels.
The conclusion was in all these cases the elevator companies had taken No. 2, and No. 3, and No. 4, northern and mixed it with No. 1 northern and consequently shipped out far more No. 1 northern than they had taken in.

In order to support that contention, let me

I desire to say a few words on this resolution before it is passed, as the subject affects not only the west but the whole Dominion. It is usually supposed that the farmers in the west are extremely prosperous, and can stand any kind of thing as regards tariff charges and so on. But let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer of the west is up against a good many things. He is, as it were, a partner of nature; he supplies the labour, and nature supplies the soil and climate. But nature is sometimes very unkind to him, and occasionally we have too much rain and sometimes too little. Sometimes we have a devastating hail storm which wipes out all chance of crops that year. At other times, a frost visits the fields before the grain is mature, and ripens it in fact before it is properly filled. This accounts for the different qualities of wheat. Now, I think the farmer is perfectly ready to accept any chances where he cannot control them. But I do not think he is at all willing to accept the extortions of the middlemen and others who are handling his grain, and who are simply watching the farmer to see how much grain he is raising in oTder that they may see how much they can make out of him when he sells his grain. The farmer is.willing to pay all legitimate charges and costs of hauling and handling. But there is a class of men, owners or lessees of the terminal elevators, who, it is well , proved, are in the habit of manipulating the farmers' grain to their own pecuniary advantage, and at the expense of the reputation of his wheat. While my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) was speaking, an hon. member asked him how this kind of thing is done, and my hon. friend replied that not being a farmer, he [DOT]could not exactly say, but referred his questioner to a farmer. Now I happen to be a farmer, and I may say that I do not know

exactly how this is done; I think the only man that can tell is the grain manipulator himself. He has got the science down pretty fine. But I understand it is something like this. The grain is graded into piobaibly six or seven different qualities. The qualities are established by purity, by colour, and by weight. Now if the grain buyer gets in a number of cars of different qualities of wheat, he will take some small quantity of the best grade and mix it with inferior grades so as to bring them up probably to the weight of an intermediate grade; and consequently he will get a bigger price for that grade. I have seen a great many farmers who have gone to the old country and have interviewed millers there. They have taken to the old country samples of our wheat, and have been informed by the millers there that they rarely ever saw wheat of that quality in the old country, if they did they were willing to _ pay a good price for it. One of my neighbours took a sample of No. 2 Northern which he had grown himself, and showed it to a miller in the old country, who told him that he rarely saw wheat of that quality, but lie would be willing to pay a good price for it if he could get it. He gave my friend a sample of what he bought" as No. 2, and when he came back to this country he showed it to the inspector who graded it as No. 4. Now that grain had been mixed m this way, and in this way we are losing the value of our wheat. When a miller looks at a sample of grain he says. This will make so much flour, it may be a No. 2 or No. 3, and we will fix the price at so much according to its milling value. Now if it is an inferior sample, if it is No. 2 or No. 3, yet inferior in milling qualities, the price is fyjed lower. So they never really get our wheat in the shape in which it leaves the fanners' loading platform, or the local elevator.
What remedy should there be to prevent this kind of thing? I think it will bo acknowledged that it exists. A system of government inspection was inaugurated and I am of opinion that to a certain extent it was successful although a great many are of a different opinion. I base my judgment upon the facts ascertained and the conclusions arrived at which proved conclusively that this manipulating was going on. It took some time to find this out. The government inspectors could tell the quality of the grain going out but they could not tell whether that was due to mixing or whether the grain came originally from the farmers in that shape, and until the stocks in the elevators got low no comparison could be made. When the stocks got low, the balance of the grain was weighed and graded, and then it was found that this manipulation had been going on. Several of those

Like the hon. member for Begina (Mr. Martin), I am not particularly in love with the idea of the government operating everything in sight. I think the functions of government are something different and that it is the duty and the privilege of private citizens to carry on the commerce and business of the country. But sometimes such government interference is necessary, and this may be such a case. At all events, it would give satisfaction to the farmers of the west, who are very uneasy owing to the existing state of affairs. If the terminal elevators were operated by the government, I think probably it would be the best plan. Under the present system there are a large number of inspectors and they are paid out of the general revenue. If the government purchased or leased these elevators, and the inspectors, who are expert grain men, were turned into operators, the cost of their salaries and rentals and insurance, &c., could be made a charge against the wheat. In that way a great deal of money would be saved and every one who raises any wheat is perfectly willing that all legitimate charges should come out of the wheat. I think also that a man should accompany every vessel loaded with wheat going to Port Colborne or Buffalo, and that he should accompany that wheat until it reaches the sea-going vessel, after which it could not be tampered with.
However, my reason for addressing the House is to point out the absolute necessity for a remedy that will be really effective. It is quite possible, I think it is quite probable, that the only system and the better system is for the government to take over the elevators either by purchase or lease and operate them under a commission. I believe that leasing would be best in the beginning. As a farmer, representing a farming community, I wish to place myself on record as* being in great sympathy with this question. I know that these abuses have been going on, I know that very serious losses have occurred all through the west, it does not affect the east, I suppose, in the same way, but it certainly does affect the west as every western man knows. The problem is to provide a remedy, and I re-

iterate my belief that government operation under a commission would be the best. As there are other members who may wish to speak on this subject at length and as under the rules of the House this debate must close at six o'clock and may possibly not be resumed this session,

I simply want to place myself on record as being strongly in favour of an effective system which will prevent the improper admixture of the farmer's grain. He is entitled to the market value of what he grows, less the cost of transportation, &c. Every one will admit that he is not getting that under the present system and therefore it is absolutely necessary that some better system be thought out and applied. I have much pleasure in seconding the motion.

Up to that point we have no quarrel with him; we have only to say that these matters have been brought to the attention of the House by hon. gentlemen on this side for some years back, that this abuse is now recognized on all hands as existing, and that the injustice of it has appealed to all sections of the country. So there was no necessity whatever of further impressing parliament with its importance because the First Minister in this House has already laid it down that there was an abuse that
demanded a remedy. To that extent I cannot see that the hon. gentleman has accomplished much. His position in relation to the various remedies suggested, as I understand it, is this: He says he sees no reason why government control should not be successful; he advises, as he did some two years ago, the enforcement of the Grain Act as a solution, if that succeeds. He sees no reason why control by a commission without government ownership or operation should not be successful and he favours that, if that succeeds. And lastly he says that while he is personally adverse to the whole principle of government ownership and operation he believes it is a case for government ownership and operation and he also favours that, if it succeeds. So that, the hon. gentleman's cogitations lasting doubtless over many years has brought him at last to this remarkable point, that in a moment of daring he is willing to assure this House that whatever solution will be a success he is in favour of it. I must commend to the attention of parliament and the country the very great political enterprise of the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin). There was a meeting in a rural school district some years ago and the subject of discussion was what should be done with the school house in the cold winter months. In reference to the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin), I am convinced that the government of this country is fust as anxious to settle this question satisfactorily and in the best interests of the people of this country as the most enthusiastic and ardent supporter of western interests can possibly be. I heard the Premier of Canada, during his western tour last summer, make the statement, in answer to deputations of farmers who waited upon him, that as far as the question of terminal elevators was concerned, his government had put their hand to the plough, and they would not turn back until they had remedied the grievances complained of under present conditions. As to the method, he did not say that his government had decided what it should be, but he was prepared to go the length of government ownership and operation, if necessary, if that were the only remedy that could be afforded. We must remember that there are a great many things that may militate against the success of the farmers' operations. Many
years ago, as my hon. friend from Regina intimated* the conditions of the grain trade in western Canada were very serious indeed. As a result of those conditions the farmers of the west became organized, and year after year they have come to Ottawa to lay their views beiore the government of the day in regard to the proper remedies for the evils that existed. The result has been that for many years past there has been an evolution in the grain laws of this country, an evolution, we confidently believe, wholly in the interest of the producer of grain. The establishment of a loading platform, the bringing into existence of the inspection of gram at Winnipeg, the introduction of government supervision and control at the terminal elevators at Port William and Port Arthur, have undoubtedly tended very largely to improve the conditions of the grain trade, and in recent years -in the last year, in fact-other changes have been brought about which, to my mind, have been responsible for a very great change in the grain trade of western Canada. I refer to the establishment at Port William and Port Arthur of a clearing house, which was not in existence when this question was discussed in this House two sessions ago. Perhaps some hon. members will recall that on that occasion I called the attention of the House to one great loss from which the grain trade wat suffering, in the fact that vessels which came to the terminals at Fort William and Port Arthur to obtain loads required two or three times as long to load at those ports as they did at American ports, because of the absence of a clearing house. During the following summer the Department of Trade and Commerce, in agreement with the terminal interests at Port Arthur, established a clearing house, with the result that to-day, instead of finding great shortages on our Canadian shipping routes and a great loss of time in loading at Port William and Port Arthur, the conditions are very much more satisfactory at these ports than they are at ports on the other side of the boundary in the same line of business.

It was established some time in the summer of 1909. It appears to me to be a very plain proposition that anything that causes loss or waste in the grain trade must affect the price to the farmer, and anything that stops the leaks from the time the grain leaves the farmer to the time it reaches its market must increase the price of the grain. The differences in the figures with regard to the shortages at the ports

across the line, and at our own terminals at Port William and Port Arthur, and on the lakes, are very remarkable indeed. The average shortage at Chicago during the last season was 22 pounds of wheat to the 1,000 bushels; at Milwaukee it was 22 pounds. The smallest loss from any American port was 11 pounds per 1,000 bushels. At Fort William and Port Arthur there was actually a surplus of 2 pounds per 1,000 bushels shipped, and that is undoubtedly due to the establishment of the clearing house, which enables the government officials at these ports to fix any shortage at its proper place, and thus bring about a remedy.
I say that there is, in connection with this clearing house, a registration bureau at Fort William and Port Arthur, and this has been a very great step in advance as far as the remedying of the evils of the grain trade is concerned. With regard to this registration bureau, there may be those not familiar with the grain trade who may not understand its objects and effects, and I may point out that although there was a prosecution of a terminal elevator company for having made false returns during the season of 1909, or for having mixed grain, I have not heard of any serious complaints with regard to this season's operation from the purchasers of grain, especially from Fort William or Port Arthur. I have not heard of any complaints regarding the handling of grain at these points, and I think that one of the chief reasons for this improvement is the establishing of a registration bureau at Fort William. The object of this bureau is this, and it has this purpose and effect, that just as soon as an elevator gets a car load of No. 1 Northern wheat, the shipper comes to this registration official, who is called the registrar, who acts partly as a government official and also in the' interests of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and whose interests, so far as the terminal elevators are concerned, are identical with those of the western farmer. This registrar gives a receipt for the amount of No, 1 or No. 2 Northern, as the case may be, which the elevator man has received in car lots and has put into his elevator. This must correspond with the grade of wheat certificate furnished Ibiy the government weighmaster and inspector. When the elevator man wishes to ship out a certain quantity of No. 1 or No. 2 Northern, he must go to the registrar, and the registrar cancels his receipts to the extent of the amount shipped. When the elevator man is compelled to register with the registration bureau the amount of each particular grade of grain which he takes into his elevator and when that must correspond with the grade of wheat certificate of the government inspector and weighmaster, and when before he can ship out of his elevator any amount of any grade of grain, he must Mr. NEELY.
cancel the certificates or receipts with the registrar to the extent of the amount he ships out, can any one tell me how, at the end of the season, it is possible for that man to get away with mixing the grain at those terminals. What would be the benefit P If, for instance, he gets in 10,000 bushels of No. 1 Northern at the end of the season he has cancelled receipts or certificates to that effect, and the inspector goes into his bins and finds 100,000 more bushels No. 1 Northern in them-why it seems absurd a man should undertake operations that lay him immediately open to the clutches of the law. My hon. friends may ask how has it been done before. As a matter of fact this bureau was only established the past season, and since its establishment I have not heard of any serious complaint along the lines of those made in past years.
But there are dozens of other ways in which harm may come to the grain trade, apart from that which came in former years through the operations of these terminals at Port Arthur and Fort William. Take a case of this kind. A short time ago, in conversation with a wholesale baker who purchased flour which he supposed to have been made from wheat of a certain grade, he gave me this information. He was purchasing his flour from a certain miller in Ontario, supposing it to have been made from No. 2 Northern wheat. He found however, that the flour was very bad and not at all what it ought to be. So one day he took a trip to the mill and discovered that the miller was grinding out wheat that averaged No. 4 instead of No. 2 and was selling the flour as No. 2. He went to the miller and charged him with dishonesty, but the miller said that is the wheat I 'got for N^o. 2. Now I am absolutely convinced that it was not what that miller got for No.
2.	Here is the situation. We have an inspection at Port Arthur and Fort William, but the man who is shipping the grain from those points to any point in Ontario, for instance, says to the seller:	I do not
want you to put the grade oi that grain on your bill of lading. The wheat then comes down to Ontario without any grade marked on the bill of lading, and the miller, in the instance I have cited, _ may possibly have done this. He may have taken an old grade certificate, a No. 2 grade certificate, and have held that certificate instead of destroying it, and he may have shown that to the baker and have said to him: Here is the grade certificate for the wheat I am grinding into flour for you, when that wheat probably came to him without any grade certificate at all. There you find a side light on this question which shows us that after all the serious trouble in the grain situation, which in years past was at Fort William and Port Arthur, extends today to every point throughout Canada

where there is a transfer elevator. We must also remember that a considerable quantity of our wheat goes through the United States. The wheat that goes by the United States we have absolutely no control over from the moment it reaches an American port. The United States refuse to bond our wheat by the grade, they merely bond the quantity, so that in the case of wheat shipped to Buffalo or any other American port, all the shipper is responsible for is the quantity and not the quality, so that wheat of ours may reach the Liverpool market in a demoralized condition as the result of mixture that goes on across the line. I point this out simply to show that all the trouble is not centred, as some hon. members would suggest, at Fort William and Port Arthur, but that the whole grain trade of Canada is in such a position that the operator in grain who wishes to destroy the quality and grade of our grain as these grades are passed through the inspectors' hands at Winnipeg and Fort William has abundant field in any part of Canada. I call attention to these points to show that the question, after all, is not so simple as it might at first appear, and also to call the attention of the government to the fact that any schemes they may introduce-and as. I said before, I am satisfied it is their intention to bring in something that will be satisfactory, that will touch the heart of the question-should have cognizance of the grain from the time it leaves the market at the farmers' door until it reaches Liverpool and other world market points.
My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie, (Mr. Meighen), has suggested that there is one remedy for the evils of the grain trade, and that is government ownership and operation. I believe that, before we can have successful government ownership and operation, if that be the necessary solution, we must have men trained to the operating of the terminal and transfer elevators. Thus, in my opinion, the very first step in the solution of this difficult question is the appointment of a commission as suggested by my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin). That hon. gentleman was asked as to the sort of commission he would favour, and I may very well be asked the same question. My answer would be that I would favour a commission with the very widest powers possible, so far as the handling of the grain trade is concerned. I would favour a commission that would hold the same relation toward the grain trade as the Board of Railway Commissioners holds toward the railways. Such legislation would not be entirely new, for such a commission already exists in the State of Minnesota, where, I believe, the conditions of the grain trade are probably more satisfactory than in any other part of North America. They have what they call a warehouse and grain
commission which has powers and relations to the grain trade much the same as those held by the Canadian Board of Railway Commissioners in relation~to the railways of Canada. The members of this proposed new commission should be men thoroughly versed in the grain situation. And they should be given wide powers; for, if they are the right stamp of men, they can be trusted with such powers. And they should have a length of appointment that would ensure them freedom from any political or partisan influence for a considerable number of years. They should not be subject in any way to corporation influence or control. Get such a commission, give them the powers I have indicated, and it would be in their province to make regulations governing the grain trade, not merely at the terminals, but in every part of Canada, including the Atlantic and Pacific seaports and also our future port on Hudson bay. I would go even further and give them power to send agents abroad to learn of the condition in which Canadian grain is reaching the markets of the world. I have already shown that our grain going through American channels is subject to being tampered with. That is a state of affairs that we could not directly remedy; but, if we had such a commission as I speak of, though they could not control that situation, at least they could notify the purchasers, or would-be purchasers of Canadian grain, that if they wished to secure Canadian grai'' pure and intact, as it left the inspection department at Winnipeg or at Fort William, they must specify that that grain must pass by all-Canadian routes. That also would be a very important matter that would tend very largely to raise the standard of our grain in the markets of the world. If such a commission were inaugurated, it would be one of their main objects, after having thoroughly familiarized themselves with the conditions as they exist, to come to a conclusion as to the best method of handling the terminal and transfer elevators. The views of this commission would be invaluable as to the necessity or otherwise of government ownership and operation.
Now, I am not prepared to advocate views simply because they are the views of somebody else; and, while all my sympathy goes out to the farmer, not only the farmer of the west, but all the farmers who in the past, have been subject to loss through manipulation of their grain, I must first be convinced that government ownership and operation is essentially and vitally necessary to remedy the evil. It is a very simple proposition, some hon. members would suggest, or may think, to take the step, to go into government owner-shin. Yes, but if it does not work well, it will be very hard to get out of it. Hon.
)

members must remember that the grain trade of Canada is only in its infancy. We talk of the large quantities of grain that have been shipped from western Canada within the last couple of years. Why, we are only on the fringe of things in the great west. So, if we take such a step today, no matter how sincere we may he, no matter how much we may think it in the interests of the grain producer, if what we do militates in the end against the grain trade, the evil resulting will grow with the years. Therefore, I say, it behooves us to go carefully. Insistent-as I a.m aware- as are the demands of the farmers of the west for the speedy remedy, and loud as some of them declaim that the only remedy is government ownership and operation, I am free to say that my advice to the government on this occasion would be to consider with the greatest care every step that they take on this question. If they .make a mistake now, if they start out on a certain line of policy and that proves not to be *what they expected, the harmful results in years to come would be inestimable.
Now, I want to call the attention of my hon. friends who are so strongly in favour of government ownership to one or two features of the government ownership and operation of terminal elevators, and other utilities of this kind. The large financial responsibility involved in the expropriation or purchase of the terminal and transfer elevators of this country is not a thing to be waived lightly aside. We must remember, as I have already remarked, that while at the present moment this would involve an enormous outlay of money, in the days to come when new seaports^ are established in Canada, and our grain trade increases, this will involve an ever increasing 'expenditure on the part of the government. I am not saving that the country is not rich enough to do this. I am simply reminding the House that we must not consider as a question of no moment the taking over of these elevators. There is another feature in this question. We might possibly have some difficulty in getting hold, of these elevators, it might ultimately mean expropriation. I want to ask my hon. friends who are in favour of this principle if they consider that drastic measures of that kind at the present stage of Canada's development __form the best method we can adopt to induce foreign capital to come into this country for its development. The other day we heard a member of this House speak very strongly in favour of bringing our railways to account by reason of their excessive rates. These excessive rates probably exist to some extent, how far we do not know. But there is this to remember. The people of western Canada are so anxious to get Mr. NEELY.
railroads at the present time, no matter whose capital builds them, that I am quite certain the majority of the people would prefer to pay even excessive rates rather than have no railway transportation at all. So I say that we must be a little cautious how we proceed lest we discourage the investment of foreign capital in the enterprises that are necessary to develop this great country.
Another thing I would refer to the consideration of those who believe that government ownership and operation is the only principle to adopt. Any system that is adopted must be a flexible system. By that I mean that there must he no obstacle put in the way of the natural and easy flow of grain in the channels of trade as they now exist in Canada. I have already pointed out that it is essential that so far as possible we retain our Canadian trade in Canadian channels that is to say, we must encourage the shippers and buyers to ship grain by all Canadian routes if they wish the identity of that grain to be preserved until it reaches the markets of the world. Now, let this government undertake to impose conditions at the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur that will make the burden of shipping via those points onerous on the grain dealers, what will be the natural result? The natural result will be that trade will follow the lines of least resistance, and instead of the bulk of our grain going by Canadian ports as it does at present, we will find it directed towards American ports ; the grain will lose its identity, and we will lose the benefit of having it go by an all Canadian route. Take for instance, our customs and our post office administrations. We understand that there must be rules laid down for any government institution, and that it must be operated strictly according to those rules. You cannot leave everything at the discretion of the official who is operating. So conditions might arise under government ownership and operation that might be onerous to the man who is dealing in grain, and if that occurs once or twice in the experience of a grain dealer, the result will be that he will transfer the field of his operations to some place where conditions are not so onerous. Now, I am not suggesting that we should make the grain trade so flexible that the grain dealer can do what he likes with his grain ; that is not the point at all. I am referring simply to the problem of transportation, of getting the grain from the farmer's home to the markets of the world with as little friction and trouble as possible.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest, in solution of this question, a method that will preserve the quality of the grain intact from the time it leaves the government

inspector at Winnipeg and Fort William until it reaches the markets of the world. I say again that government ownership and operation of the terminals and transfefr elevators further east alone will not prove a solution of this difficulty, if, indeed, it be necessary at all to a solution of the question. This commission I suggest should have very large powers; they should be able, like the Railway Commission, to deal with every feature and phase of the grain trade from the initial elevator right through so far as our Canadian jurisdiction extends. There is no manner of doubt that to-day our law is too lenient. The men who in the past have been manipulating grain, making an improper admixture, under regulations less severe than we have to-day, have undoubtedly got off too light. The laws of the state of Minnesota are much more severe than are ours in regard to the penalties imposed. The question has been asked: What penalties should be fixed by a commission for elevator operators who break the laws? Unfortunately, many of the owners of our terminal elevators are not citizens of Canada; they reside in the United States, outside the jurisdiction of our law. The only remedy I can think of for that condition is that every elevator company operating at terminal points in Canada should be compelled to name and bond some prominent Canadian citizen, some business man on this side of the line, who would personally be responsible for the operation of their elevators. It would not be sufficient that the man who operates the elevator at a salary x>f, perhaps, $3,000 or $4,000 a year should suffer a penalty of 5 or 10 years' imprisonment for infractions of the law, there should be some substantial individual named as the representative of the company operating the elevator, and that person should be made responsible for any infraction of the law to the extent of any fine that may be imposed, as well as to imprisonment for that infraction. There is even a further penalty that may be imposed, cancellation of the license for a year or two years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say to some of the hon. members who have been discussing this question that the trouble is not altogether with the terminal elevators. It is the general representation that there is a good deal of manipulation going on in these elevators. I happened to be in the House when the delegation of western farmers was here and I heard their arguments. The difficulty arises very largely long before the grain reaches the terminal elevators and it is a defect in part in the legislation. I believe that when the grain reaches Winnipeg, and it may be there purchased by A, B and C and transferred to the local elevators. I do not know what the practice may be to-day as there may have been some recent change within the last few months. It is not inspected into these elevators although samples are taken, but it is inspected when it comes out of the elevators and it is reinspected at the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. That leaves the door open for any amount of manipulation, it permits the operator to mix it as much as he pleases, to buy a low grade and to mix with it a certain amount of a higher grade and bring it out so it will all pass out as a higher grade. That cannot take place at the terminal elevator for the reason that the grain is inspected into the elevator and out of the elevator. According to the regulations the elevator company cannot give out a greater quantity of any particular grade than their records will show they have taken in. There ought to be no great difficulty in protecting the grain at the terminal elevator or elsewhere if the regulations go far enough. Under our banking system, there is no trouble to turn up the records at any time and find howT a man's bank account stands, his deposits and audits, and so with the grain trade there could not be this manipulation if the regulations are enforced and proper records kept. I am not prepared to say that the regulations may not be im-Mr. SCHAFFNEE.
proved, I am assuming they are sufficient if they are enforced. The only possible manipulation that could possibly take place at the terminal elevator is, that the inspector might say: This grain should be cleaned to a certain extent. It is graded No. 1 or No. 2 Northern provided a certain amount of small grain and waste material is eliminated, and if that full quantity is not taken from it then the grain will measure out more bushels than the certificate will show and to that extent there might be manipulation to the value of these few extra bushels of grain. I believe that has been frequently done, but it is an evil that could readily be prevented. I have not had an opportunity of reading the hon. gentle- . man's motion, and I am, therefore, perhaps at a loss in speaking to it, but I may say that the remedy would not be applied within a reasonable time by the taking over of the elevators under government control. The obje.ct of that is to remove temptation by having the staff in these elevators disinterested so that there would be no motive for the manipulation which now takes place. Well, Sir, I cannot see wherein there would be better protection for the public in that respect than there is to-day under the system of examination if the regulations are made properly workable, and if they are properly enforced. In that respect I fanoy I agree more or less with the last speaker. Now, there is a good deal more than the terminal elevators to be considered. Grain is not inspected through all the country elevators; the grain buyers put their grain into the elevators in the country; they need not route it to Winnipeg; they may route it through to the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William, and in that case I admit there is very little if any opportunity for manipulation after the grain is shipped. But they may mix the grain previous to shipping it; they may say: Here, I can buy this at No. 1 Northern and this at No. 2, and this at No. 3. In my opinion these grains ought to be graded out No. 1, arid they may be mixed, and if the buyer is a good judge he may get the No. 1 grade for the wrhole bulk of the grain he has purchased, and that does frequently happen. Then, as to our milling companies; the milling companies at Winnipeg, and Kenora, and Fort William, and all other points have their own elevators and they buy the grain without any restriction whatever as the regulations do not relate to them at all. They can mix it as much as they like, and they can grind the inferior grade or the better grades just as they please. The questioh is a very wide one, and if it is to be dealt with at all it seems to me there ought to be some system of dealing with it all along the line.
Now, there is another question in connection with this matter; there are certain elevators at different points in the country

that do not deal with custom grain at all; they are built by certain men for the purpose of handling their own grain. I am aware that there is a question of some dispute just now as to whether an individual or a company should be allowed to carry on that business. I am not going to discuss that question because it is considerably involved and there is perhaps a good deal to be said on both sides, but at first blush it does seem to me that it is rather an extreme measure to say to any company or person: you shall not put machinery into a building to clean the grain that you may purchase. I believe the whole question of the protection of the farmer who produces grain can be worked out by proper regulations, if these regulations are wide enough and broad enough and extend not to one, but to all points, and are enforced. If the door is left open at one point for a continuance of the evil it is sought to remedy, then the door will be left open for manipulation all along the line, and I do not believe that a remedy can be applied in that way.

The trouble is that the terminal elevators have got out of the hands of the railways. As long as they were in the hands of the railways there was no great dissatisfaction. The Canadian Pacific railway always handled their elevators
well. In Fort William and Port Arthur, that company always gave very good satisfaction. There used to be some objection to the charges made for the handling of wheat, but there was never any charge that the terminal elevators, owned and operated by the Canadian Pacific railway, ever tried to do the farmers up for the benefit of the dealers. Later on, however, _ when the Canadian Northern railway built its elevators in Port Arthur, it leased the operation to Americans, who have subsidiary companies all through the west and own hundreds of elevators in all parts of the three _ prairie provinces. There is where the difficulty originated. The trouble has been that they use their opportunities to the great disadvantage of the farmers. There is no doubt in my mind that some of the regulations made during the past year by the Department of Trade and Commerce are a long step in the right direction. It has been pointed out to me by men in the grain trade this winter that now it is most difficult for any of these terminal elevators-no matter how anxious they may be to do wrong- to do so without being caught. But here I want to say that I do not believe you can watch them successfully. They will find some way of getting around the law. What we want in the west, what the western farmer and the Ontario millers, and the exporters want, is to be able to buy 100 cars of No. 3 Northern wheat and he sure of getting that grade. The western farmer is a reasonable man, he has never objected to paying for inspection, or weighing, or for freight charges. He is quite prepared to pay all the charges on every bushel of wheat he sjiips. So the government could take hold of these elevators and run very little risk of making any losses, because it is a much simpler matter to deal with than most other public utilities. But I want to point out that there are some serious objections to the government taking over these elevators. You may go ahead at present and build a new elevator with reinforced concrete, or brick, or of some fire-proof material; but you can operate that elevator so much more cheaply than the old elevators built ten, fifteen or twenty years ago, at Port Arthur and Fort William, that if the owners of those old elevators were to hand them over to the government as a present, the government could not run them any cheaper than they could build up-to-date new elevators, and make the other charges. -
